paragraphs: The paper studies how to regularize least-squares temporal difference learning, or LSTD, when approximating value functions in reinforcement learning. A central concern is choosing useful features from a potentially large collection. Regularization based on the L1 penalty encourages sparse solutions, allowing many feature weights to become zero and making it attractive for this purpose.

Applying this idea to LSTD is more complicated than applying it to ordinary regression. LSTD solves a fixed-point problem, so a regularization method must fit that structure. Existing combinations can introduce additional requirements or drawbacks; the abstract identifies the P-matrix assumption used by LASSO-TD as one example.

The authors introduce an alternative that combines LSTD with the Dantzig Selector. They investigate its performance and connections to other regularized approaches, showing that it avoids some drawbacks of existing solutions. The contribution is a different route to sparse value-function approximation that accounts for the structure of temporal difference learning, rather than treating its integration with regularization as straightforward.
icml-2012-a-dantzig-selector-approach-to.tldr: Combining LSTD with the Dantzig Selector offers a route to sparse value-function approximation that overcomes some drawbacks of existing regularized methods.

paragraphs: Item-neighbourhood recommendation methods predict a user's rating by combining that user's ratings of similar items. These similarities form a weighted graph: items are nodes, and connections indicate which items help predict one another. The paper turns this graph into an undirected probabilistic model called item fields.

Its prediction rule extends the usual neighbourhood calculation by incorporating information beyond immediate connections. This makes the graph useful as a connected system, rather than only as a collection of local weighted averages. The authors report that their approach achieves its best results with drastically fewer edges than other neighbourhood methods, suggesting that broader information can make a sparse graph effective.

The paper also develops an approximate maximum entropy training procedure using the Bethe approximation. A new decomposition breaks training into tractable subproblems. With sufficient statistics already computed on Movielens, the method reports a two-orders-of-magnitude advantage over maximum likelihood approaches in the training comparison. That qualification matters: the reported advantage is tied to the precomputed-statistics setting.
icml-2012-a-graphical-model-formulation-.tldr: Item fields extend neighbourhood recommendation with non-local graph information and an efficient approximate maximum entropy training method.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning combines different measures of similarity, potentially bringing together feature representations from several data sources. Bayesian approaches offer a framework for learning these combinations, but their computational demands have made large collections of kernels difficult to handle. This paper targets that obstacle directly.

The authors construct a fully conjugate Bayesian formulation and derive a deterministic variational approximation for inference. The formulation is designed so that the probabilistic components work together in a computationally manageable way. This enables efficient combinations of hundreds or thousands of kernels. The paper also outlines extensions to multiclass learning and learning with both labeled and unlabeled data.

Experiments involving large kernel collections report inference times below one minute on the benchmark datasets considered. On one bioinformatics dataset and three image-recognition datasets, the method also improves generalization over previously reported results. Together, these findings support the approach as a way to make large Bayesian kernel combinations practical while retaining useful predictive performance in the tested applications.
icml-2012-bayesian-efficient-multiple-ke.tldr: A conjugate Bayesian formulation and variational inference make learning combinations of hundreds or thousands of kernels computationally practical.

paragraphs: The paper considers classification when the initial list of classes does not cover everything that may arrive later. A system must recognize known categories while remaining able to discover and model new ones. The proposed framework combines these activities during online inference, updating its interpretation as observations arrive.

A Dirichlet process prior links known and unknown class distributions through a shared base distribution. This gives existing and emerging categories a common probabilistic foundation. The prior is paired with a suitable data model to support discovery of potentially interesting class groupings. Sequential Monte Carlo sampling provides the mechanism for carrying out inference as the data accumulate.

The framework specifically accounts for situations in which observations from a new class increase rapidly. The motivating biodetection application involves a previously unseen pathogen appearing and producing a growing number of samples, potentially indicating an outbreak. The contribution is a framework that treats this accumulation as part of class discovery and modeling, rather than requiring every future category to be specified beforehand.
icml-2012-bayesian-nonexhaustive-learnin.tldr: A Bayesian online framework combines classification of known categories with discovery and modeling of rapidly emerging classes.

paragraphs: The paper distinguishes two goals for actively choosing which points to label. Active search seeks to find as many members of a target class as possible. Active surveying seeks to estimate the proportion belonging to that class. In both cases, accurate general-purpose classification is secondary to the specific information the queries should deliver.

Using Bayesian decision theory, the authors choose utility functions for these objectives and derive optimal querying policies. They also prove that looking further ahead can matter enormously: less-myopic approximations can outperform more-myopic ones by an arbitrarily large amount. This establishes the possibility of a large advantage, rather than saying that additional lookahead always yields such gains.

Computing an optimal policy naively requires exploring an exponential search space. For certain models, the paper derives bounds that reduce this search while preserving optimal decisions. These reductions can be dramatic in practice and allow deeper lookahead. The work therefore connects a clear statement of the querying objective with both optimal decision rules and a way to make some of those rules more computationally accessible.
icml-2012-bayesian-optimal-active-search.tldr: Bayesian decision rules align active queries with finding target examples or estimating their prevalence, with bounds that enable deeper optimal lookahead for certain models.

paragraphs: The paper studies decision-making in passive partially observable Markov decision processes. In this setting, the agent cannot change how the world's state evolves through its actions, but its choices still incur costs. The planning problem therefore concerns choosing well under uncertainty about a world whose evolution the agent does not control.

An information-processing limit prevents the agent from keeping a complete belief about the hidden state. It must maintain an approximation instead. The central question becomes which information deserves to be retained when the purpose of that information is to support lower-cost decisions. This connects the representation of uncertainty directly to the agent's decision objective.

The authors present a variational principle for retaining the information most useful for minimizing cost, together with a simple, efficient algorithm for finding an optimum. The contribution gives a principled way to approach belief approximation under processing constraints. Its scope is the passive setting: actions have costs, but they do not alter the underlying world state.
icml-2012-bounded-planning-in-passive-po.tldr: A variational approach helps information-limited agents retain the belief information most useful for minimizing costs in passive POMDPs.

paragraphs: In multilabel classification, an example can have several relevant labels, and the goal here is to rank those labels appropriately. A common training strategy replaces ranking loss with an easier convex objective defined over pairs of labels. The paper starts from a negative theoretical result showing inconsistency of that pairwise surrogate approach.

The authors establish a positive result for a simpler alternative: common convex binary-classification losses applied to individual labels can be consistent for ranking-loss minimization. This means that optimizing an appropriate single-label surrogate can remain aligned with the desired ranking objective, despite avoiding direct training on label pairs.

The analysis goes beyond establishing eventual consistency. It derives regret bounds and convergence rates, giving a quantitative relationship between learning progress and ranking performance. The resulting losses suggest efficient, scalable algorithms, which the authors evaluate experimentally. The central finding is that a seemingly more direct pairwise formulation need not offer the stronger theoretical foundation; simpler individual-label losses can provide the consistency and quantitative guarantees sought for this task.
icml-2012-consistent-multilabel-ranking-.tldr: Common convex losses applied to individual labels can consistently optimize multilabel rankings, with regret bounds and convergence rates.

paragraphs: Electronic medical records contain relationships among patients, medications, diseases, and health events. Predicting a future adverse drug reaction requires handling both these connections and uncertainty about how past health relates to future outcomes. Statistical relational learning combines relational and probabilistic representations, making it a natural approach to this kind of prediction.

The difficulty addressed here is latent structure: related medications or diseases may share useful patterns that are not directly represented. Clustering can expose those groupings, but choosing groups before learning separates that decision from the prediction task. The proposed method instead builds clusters as they are needed during learning, allowing the learning process to guide which groupings become useful.

The authors evaluate the approach on three real-world tasks that predict adverse medication reactions from medical records. It achieves higher accuracy than learning without clustering, clustering in advance, and using expert-built medical heterarchies. These findings support task-guided clustering as a useful way to represent hidden relationships in the evaluated medical prediction settings.
icml-2012-demand-driven-clustering-in-re.tldr: Clustering medications and diseases during learning improves adverse-drug-reaction prediction across three evaluated medical-record tasks.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes Gaussian process bandit optimization when function evaluations are deterministic. The learner searches for a global maximum using observations of an unknown objective. Its performance is expressed through regret, which measures the shortfall associated with the search relative to the optimum.

The analysis uses a branch-and-bound algorithm related to upper-confidence-bound optimization. It complements an earlier result for observations with strictly positive Gaussian noise, where regret decreases at approximately the inverse square root of the number of observations. By focusing on the deterministic setting, the authors obtain a substantially faster asymptotic rate.

Under regularity assumptions, they prove with high probability that regret decreases as O(exp(-τt/(ln t)^(d/4))). Here, t is the observation count, d is the search-space dimension, and τ depends on the objective's behavior near its global maximum. The expression describes exponential decay modified by a logarithmic factor. The result highlights how much stronger convergence guarantees can become without observation noise, while retaining explicit dependence on dimension, local objective behavior, and the stated assumptions.
icml-2012-exponential-regret-bounds-for-.tldr: For deterministic Gaussian process observations, a branch-and-bound analysis gives a high-probability, near-exponential regret decay rate under regularity assumptions.

paragraphs: Selecting a hidden Markov model involves deciding how much hidden-state structure is needed to explain sequential data. This paper extends factorized asymptotic Bayesian inference, previously developed for independent hidden variables in mixture models, to hidden variables that depend on one another over time.

The method repeatedly maximizes a lower bound on a factorized information criterion. It retains several properties of the mixture-model approach: the criterion is asymptotically consistent with marginal log-likelihood, a shrinkage effect supports hidden-state selection, and iterative optimization increases the lower bound monotonically. These properties connect model selection with the procedure used to fit the model.

The approach has no tunable hyperparameter, allowing its model-selection process to be automated. In the reported experiments, it outperforms state-of-the-art variational Bayesian and nonparametric Bayesian HMM methods in both model-selection accuracy and computational efficiency. The contribution is therefore both a theoretical extension to temporal dependence and an empirically effective procedure for choosing hidden-state structure without a separate hyperparameter-tuning step.
icml-2012-factorized-asymptotic-bayesian.tldr: Factorized asymptotic Bayesian inference enables automated HMM state selection and improves selection accuracy and efficiency in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Choosing where a diffusion process should start depends on how much time it has to spread. A source set that reaches many nodes eventually may behave differently under a limited time horizon. This paper addresses that temporal aspect of influence maximization for a network whose structure and timing dynamics are given.

The authors use continuous-time Markov chains to analytically compute the expected total number of nodes reached from a chosen source set. This connects source selection to the actual timing of propagation. They then show that finding the most influential source set is NP-hard and develop an efficient approximation algorithm with a provable near-optimal performance guarantee.

Experiments on synthetic and real diffusion networks report an improvement of at least 20% over other state-of-the-art algorithms, with robustness across different network topologies. These results support explicitly modeling temporal dynamics when maximizing spread within a deadline. The theoretical guarantee and empirical comparisons address complementary questions: how close the approximation is to optimal and how it performs on the evaluated networks.
icml-2012-influence-maximization-in-cont.tldr: Continuous-time diffusion modeling supports a provably near-optimal source-selection algorithm that improves influence maximization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Online sequence prediction uses the elements already observed to predict the next one. Methods that make no assumptions about a sequence's origin can learn useful temporal structure when sequences are long. For short sequences, however, there may be too little time to learn that structure before predictions are needed.

Prediction with expert advice offers a possible remedy by combining a set of predictors. With r experts, established results allow performance close to the best expert when sequence length is on the order of log(r). The practical difficulty is obtaining a small set that contains useful experts when prior knowledge of the task is limited.

The paper introduces and analyzes an algorithm that learns the expert set from previously observed training sequences. This transfers information from earlier sequences into the collection available for predicting new ones. Experiments on web click prediction demonstrate the approach's merits. The contribution addresses the construction of the expert pool itself, a necessary practical choice behind applying expert-advice methods to short sequences.
icml-2012-learning-the-experts-for-onlin.tldr: Learning a compact set of prediction experts from past sequences helps address the difficulty of predicting short new sequences.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation becomes harder when source and target data use different feature representations, including different numbers of dimensions. Directly comparing those vectors is then problematic. This paper proposes Heterogeneous Feature Augmentation, or HFA, to make information from both domains usable within a shared learning method.

Two projection matrices map the domains into a common subspace where their examples can be compared. The method then augments each transformed representation with its original features and zeros. This combines a shared representation with information specific to each domain, producing features that existing methods such as support vector classification and regression can use.

The authors develop a linear objective using the SVM hinge loss, describe a kernelized version for very high-dimensional data, and provide an alternating optimization algorithm for the resulting problem. Experiments on two benchmark datasets show HFA outperforming existing heterogeneous domain-adaptation methods. The results support combining cross-domain comparability with retained original features as an effective approach in the evaluated settings.
icml-2012-learning-with-augmented-featur.tldr: HFA combines shared projections with original domain-specific features to learn across domains with different feature spaces.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning learns a target policy from data collected while following a different behavior policy. Actor-critic methods explicitly represent the policy, making them useful when action selection should be stochastic or the action space is large. This paper combines these two capabilities in an incremental learning algorithm.

The authors build on advances in off-policy gradient temporal-difference learning to develop an actor-critic method whose per-step computation scales linearly with the number of learned parameters. Its space requirements are also linear, and it includes eligibility traces. This makes the combination computationally manageable as the parameter count grows, while preserving explicit control over the policy representation.

The paper presents the method as the first off-policy actor-critic algorithm with this per-step scaling. It proves convergence under assumptions similar to those used for previous off-policy algorithms. On standard reinforcement-learning benchmarks, it performs better than or comparably to existing methods. The contribution is the practical combination of off-policy data use, flexible policy representation, and economical incremental updates, backed by conditional theory and empirical comparisons.
icml-2012-linear-off-policy-actor-critic.tldr: An incremental off-policy actor-critic algorithm combines flexible policy learning with linear time and space requirements and a conditional convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution through optimization, but standard methods often depend on convenient conjugacy relationships within the model. Those requirements can make an approximation difficult to derive for more general graphical models. This paper proposes a flexible approximation family inspired by nonparametric kernel density estimation.

The approximation uses multiple kernels whose locations and bandwidth are adjustable variational parameters. Optimization moves and reshapes these components to improve an approximate lower bound on the data's marginal likelihood. Having several kernels allows the approximation to represent multiple posterior modes, so it can capture several separated concentrations of probability.

The authors demonstrate the method on hierarchical logistic regression and nonlinear matrix factorization. Predictive performance matches or exceeds that of more specialized variational methods and sample-based approximations in these evaluations. The stated appeal is both representational flexibility and ease of application to models for which standard variational derivations are difficult. The results support this approach as a practical alternative without requiring the posterior approximation to concentrate around only one mode.
icml-2012-nonparametric-variational-infe.tldr: Optimized kernel-based variational approximations capture multiple posterior modes and work in models where standard conjugate approaches are difficult to derive.

paragraphs: Online learning often evaluates performance through regret, a comparison against alternative actions. This paper argues that the standard comparison becomes inadequate when an adversary can adapt to the learner's actions. It introduces policy regret as an alternative intended to measure performance more meaningfully when the environment responds to what the learner does.

In the bandit setting, the authors prove that no algorithm can guarantee sublinear policy regret against an adaptive adversary with unbounded memory. Sublinear growth would make policy regret per round diminish over time, so this impossibility result places a fundamental constraint on the desired learning guarantee.

The abstract also reports a conversion from algorithms with sublinear regret to algorithms with sublinear policy regret, with extensions to switching, internal, and swap regret. However, it labels the adversary's memory as unbounded in this positive statement too, conflicting with the preceding impossibility result. The supplied evidence therefore supports describing the proposed conversion, but does not establish a coherent memory condition under which its guarantee holds.
icml-2012-online-bandit-learning-against.tldr: The paper introduces policy regret for adaptive adversaries and proves an impossibility result, while its abstract gives conflicting memory conditions for a positive conversion result.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces an output with multiple related parts. This paper treats prediction as a time-limited search through complete candidate outputs. A learned cost function guides the search, and the system returns the lowest-cost candidate it encounters. The framework accommodates different search procedures and arbitrary structured-prediction loss functions.

The first contribution is a way to construct an effective search space using classification learning. The authors define a limited-discrepancy search space and connect its quality to the quality of learned classifiers. This provides a route for using strong classification methods to organize the alternatives explored during structured prediction.

The second contribution is a general method for learning the search-guiding cost function. Training aims to imitate the behavior of searches guided by the true loss, making the learned cost useful for the decisions the search actually makes. Across six benchmark domains, a small amount of search significantly improves on state-of-the-art performance. These results show that searching complete outputs can be useful even with a limited search budget.
icml-2012-output-space-search-for-struct.tldr: A learned search space and cost function enable short searches over complete structured outputs to improve prediction on six benchmark domains.

paragraphs: Experimental design can require learning an unknown response function while also finding inputs that produce high responses. Sequential optimization chooses one experiment at a time, using its result to guide the next choice. High-throughput settings instead run several experiments together, creating a need to balance exploration and exploitation across a whole batch.

The paper models the unknown payoff function as a sample from a Gaussian process and allows several arms to be selected in parallel each round. Its GP-BUCB algorithm extends sequential GP-UCB to this batch setting. The algorithm supplies a principled way to choose simultaneous evaluations when their outcomes are not yet available.

The authors prove that, for any fixed batch size B, cumulative regret increases over the sequential approach by only a constant factor independent of B. This provides theoretical support for parallel Bayesian global optimization without requiring the regret penalty to grow with the fixed batch size. Demonstrations on two real-world applications also support the effectiveness of the proposed batch-selection approach.
icml-2012-parallelizing-exploration-expl.tldr: GP-BUCB chooses parallel evaluation batches with a cumulative-regret increase bounded by a constant independent of batch size, for any fixed batch size.

paragraphs: Learning methods often rely on assumptions about how examples are generated. This paper studies online testing of exchangeability, seeking a valid measure of evidence against that assumption after each new example arrives. The objective is to monitor the accumulating data rather than wait until a complete dataset has been collected.

Exchangeability martingales provide the measures used for this sequential assessment. The authors extend existing techniques for constructing them and introduce a more flexible method. The contribution concerns how to build an evolving measure of incompatibility with the assumption, keeping the testing process aligned with the arrival of individual observations.

Experiments compare the approach with earlier martingale constructions on USPS and Statlog Satellite data. Existing techniques give satisfactory results on USPS, while the authors report that the new flexibility becomes necessary for the Satellite dataset. The findings therefore distinguish between settings where established constructions suffice and one where the proposed extension is needed. Overall, the method is reported to be competitive with previous martingales.
icml-2012-plug-in-martingales-for-testin.tldr: A more flexible martingale construction tests exchangeability as observations arrive and addresses a benchmark where earlier techniques were insufficient.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a binary-classification objective designed to remain robust when training labels contain errors. Its non-convex loss, called q-loss, is developed with adiabatic quantum optimization in mind. Hardware constraints shape the formulation: training becomes quadratic unconstrained binary optimization, and model parameters use low-bit-depth binary representations.

The experiments use a heuristic classical solver as a stand-in for quantum hardware. Across several popular datasets, the authors compare test error as label noise increases against existing convex and non-convex loss approaches. They report substantial robustness advantages and attribute that robustness to the non-convexity of the hardware-compatible objective.

The claimed advantage is carefully qualified. The authors do not establish theoretical superiority over other non-convex losses; those losses could perform equally well or better if solved optimally. The distinctive contribution is an objective that combines observed robustness with compatibility with the targeted quantum hardware. The experiments validate the approach through classical optimization, so they do not constitute a demonstration of quantum-computing performance.
icml-2012-robust-classification-with-adi.tldr: Quantum-hardware-compatible q-loss improves robustness to label noise in classical-solver experiments without claiming theoretical superiority over other non-convex losses.

paragraphs: The paper assumes that data lie around several manifolds, each with low intrinsic dimensionality. Under this view, the data's meaningful structure can be simpler than its full representation suggests, but different groups may follow different underlying shapes. Robust Multiple Manifold Structure Learning, or RMMSL, aims to estimate and separate those structures.

The method works at two levels. Locally, weighted low-rank matrix factorization efficiently estimates tangent spaces, describing the nearby directions of each manifold. Globally, a robust clustering method uses these local estimates. A new curved-level similarity function guides clustering toward the flattest manifold groups, making geometric structure central to how observations are grouped.

The authors compare RMMSL with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic data, handwritten digits, human motion capture, and motorbike videos. They report higher clustering accuracy and promising results for human motion segmentation and learning motion flow from video. These findings support combining local geometric estimation with global clustering under the multiple low-dimensional manifold assumption, across several evaluated types of data.
icml-2012-robust-multiple-manifold-struc.tldr: RMMSL combines local tangent-space estimation with curvature-sensitive clustering to recover multiple low-dimensional structures robustly.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis seeks a compact representation of variation in data, but contaminated observations complicate that task. This paper considers robust PCA in a high-dimensional regime where the number of observations is comparable to or greater than the dimension of each observation. It proposes a deterministic alternative to an existing randomized approach.

The new algorithm retains the theoretical properties of its randomized counterpart. These include tractability, resistance to contaminated points, compatibility with kernelization, and asymptotic consistency. It also retains the stated maximal robustness of a 50% breakdown point. These properties make robustness part of the algorithm's theoretical foundation, rather than only an observed outcome.

The principal improvement is computational efficiency: the deterministic method is reported to be significantly faster while preserving those guarantees. That combination matters for large applications, where a robust procedure must also be practical to run. The paper's contribution is therefore a more efficient way to obtain the established robust-PCA properties, with the authors identifying large-scale real applications as a suitable use.
icml-2012-robust-pca-in-high-dimension-a.tldr: A deterministic robust-PCA algorithm improves computational efficiency while retaining its randomized counterpart's guarantees, including a 50% breakdown point.

paragraphs: Scene parsing assigns an object category to every image pixel. The proposed system learns features directly from raw pixels using a multiscale convolutional network. Each pixel's representation incorporates surrounding regions of different sizes, reducing the need to manually engineer image features.

Alongside feature extraction, the system builds a tree of image segments from pixel dissimilarities. It aggregates learned features for each segment and predicts the distribution of object categories inside it. The system then selects tree nodes that cover the image while maximizing average category purity. This favors a segmentation whose regions are likely to contain a single object.

The authors report record accuracies on Sift Flow and Barcelona, with 33 and 170 classes respectively, and near-record accuracy on the eight-class Stanford Background dataset. The system is also reported to be an order of magnitude faster than competing approaches, labeling a 320-by-240 image in under one second including feature extraction. These results connect learned multiscale representations with a structured selection of coherent image regions.
icml-2012-scene-parsing-with-multiscale-.tldr: Learned multiscale features and purity-based selection of image segments deliver strong scene-parsing accuracy with fast image labeling.

paragraphs: Diffusion data often reveal when people copy information, make decisions, or become infected without revealing the network connecting those events. Recovering that hidden network is especially difficult when it changes quickly. Only a relatively small collection of cascades may be observed before the underlying structure has changed substantially.

The paper develops a scalable approximation algorithm for inferring diffusion networks in this limited-cascade setting. It provides a provable near-optimal performance guarantee and is reported to achieve high reconstruction accuracy. The work addresses an identified open problem: obtaining useful network inference while combining limited observations with the computational demands of growing networks.

Experiments use both synthetic and real diffusion data to assess accuracy and running time. The authors describe the observed balance between these objectives as optimal in practice. This empirical statement accompanies, but is distinct from, the algorithm's theoretical near-optimal guarantee. The practical significance is the ability to infer hidden propagation structure from the relatively small amount of evidence available while a network remains sufficiently stable.
icml-2012-submodular-inference-of-diffus.tldr: A scalable, provably near-optimal approximation infers hidden diffusion networks accurately from relatively small collections of cascades.

paragraphs: Words can be represented in a space as large as the vocabulary, making it useful to learn lower-dimensional representations from unlabeled text. Those representations can then supplement features in supervised tasks. This paper proposes a spectral method for learning an eigenword dictionary using canonical correlation analysis, or CCA.

The method performs CCA in two stages. First, it relates the contexts to the left and right of a word. Second, it applies CCA between the projections produced by that first step and the word itself. This uses relationships between the two context views before learning their relationship to the word representation.

The authors prove that the two-step procedure has lower sample complexity than the simple single-step alternative. That result concerns the amount of data needed to learn the representation. Experiments on part-of-speech tagging and sentiment classification illustrate the method's effectiveness and the richness of its learned representations. Together, the theory and applications support using an initial context-alignment step to improve subsequent word-representation learning.
icml-2012-using-cca-to-improve-cca-a-new.tldr: Two-step CCA first aligns left and right contexts, then relates them to words, lowering sample complexity compared with a single-step procedure.
